content.p: In July 2007 Glenn Wheatley, the Australian manager who had guided John Farnham's career since 1982, pleaded guilty in an Australian county court to three charges of tax evasion. The court case placed him among the best-known figures caught up in Operation Wickenby, the federal tax investigation that Pollstar News said was believed to be the biggest white-collar criminal investigation in Australia. He was sentenced to jail a few weeks later. The length of that sentence was disputed at the time, and it still is in the accounts written afterwards.
content.h2: From the Masters Apprentices to management
content.p: Wheatley was born in Brisbane in 1948. In the late 1960s he joined The Masters Apprentices, the rock band, which had moved to Melbourne from Adelaide, whose hits included "Turn Up Your Radio" and "Because I Love You". The Music Network says he played bass with the group from 1968 until 1972, and SBS says he played on both of those hits. Pollstar News says that when the band had management problems, he took over its business affairs, learning the work as he went.

He set up the Wheatley Organisation in 1975, and it became the vehicle for his management career. Pollstar News says he helped put together Little River Band in the late 1970s, a group it credits with nine Top 10 hits in America and sales of 25 million albums worldwide. Obituaries Australia describes the band as his first major success as a manager, and says it benefited from his knowledge of the American music business in particular.

His client list widened from there. Pollstar News names John Farnham, Delta Goodrem, Kate Ceberano and Australian Crawl among the artists he managed, and says he took on some sports clients too. He was also involved with Ausmusic, an organisation that mentored young managers and musicians, and Pollstar News says he raised about $10 million for charity over the years.

The turning point of Wheatley's career came after John Farnham replaced Glenn Shorrock as the lead singer of Little River Band in 1982. Wheatley then began managing Farnham's career as a solo artist, and Obituaries Australia says Farnham's career was not quite on the skids, though he was not particularly in favour at that point, and that Wheatley borrowed against his own home to pay for the recording of Farnham's 12th album, Whispering Jack.

That album was released in October 1986. Obituaries Australia says it spent 25 weeks at number one and has been accredited 24 times platinum by ARIA, indicating sales of more than 1.68 million copies. SBS News called it one of the biggest-selling Australian albums of all time. SBS also reported that after the first mix of "You're the Voice", the last song added to the album, Farnham went back into the recording booth; Wheatley, in an oral history published in 2014, said Farnham "sang the livin' bejesus out of it".

Wheatley's wider business did not always go as well. In his 1999 autobiography, Paper Paradise, he called one of his worst decisions the $12 million he put into The Ivy nightclub in Melbourne, which left him close to bankruptcy. Obituaries Australia says he was pulled out of that hole by promoting Farnham's Chain Reaction tour in 1990, and by a production of the rock opera Jesus Christ Superstar. Pollstar News, reporting the court case, gives a different starting point: a court was told that he began dabbling in tax fraud after nearly going bankrupt when the Pyramid insurance society collapsed and left him with large debts from a nightclub development.

In November 2006 Accountancy Age reported that the Australian Taxation Office had charged Wheatley with tax evasion. The charges were part of Operation Wickenby, which had already brought tax fraud charges against the actor Paul Hogan. Accountancy Age, citing Australian newspapers, said the charges related to a tax minimisation scheme run by the Swiss accounting firm Strachans some years earlier, and that Strachans' head, Philip Egglishaw, had been under investigation for several months.

The details given in court reporting were specific. Pollstar News said that between 1994 and 1995 Wheatley did not declare $256,410 earned from promoting Farnham's "Talk of the Town" tour, and moved the money into Swiss trusts. It also said an associate at the sports marketing firm IMG introduced him to Egglishaw, who, local media reported, helped send about $400,000 from the promotion of a 2003 boxing match between Kostya Tszyu and Jesse James Leija to Switzerland, from where it was accessed through credit cards. Pollstar News attributed that account to local media reports.
Pollstar News described Wheatley as one of four high-profile people caught in the investigation.

Wheatley pleaded guilty on 6 July 2007 to three charges relating to tax evasion. Pollstar News reported that Judge Tim Wood reserved his decision on sentence at the end of a six-hour hearing. Wheatley told the court: "It was something that I have regretted for a long, long time, and I am ashamed for what I have brought onto my family."

The prosecutor, Richard Maidment, asked for the maximum penalty of 10 years in jail. He described Wheatley as a serial tax evader. Wheatley's counsel, Robert Richter QC, took a different line. He said the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions had offered not to press for a jail term if Wheatley co-operated, and that Wheatley had agreed to act as a witness in other Operation Wickenby trials and had repaid the money the week before the plea. Richter said the DPP had allegedly reneged on the offer about a month later, and that his client had been "treated in a shabby and most duplicitous way by the DPP".

Crikey, an Australian news website, went further in a July 2007 column. It reported that a letter from the DPP dated 7 March 2006, which reneged on the arrangement, was signed by the Melbourne-based deputy director David Adsett, and that the decision to seek a custodial sentence was his. Crikey also reported that the legal team was said to be appalled at the politically charged nature of the trial. These are Crikey's claims and its sources' claims, not findings of the court.
content.h2: The sentence and the figures that differ
content.p: Pollstar News reported that on 19 July 2007 an Australian court sentenced Wheatley to 15 months in jail. It put the tax he had dodged at $318,092, saying part of his promotion fee from the 2003 bout had been routed through a sham offshore company, and that he had paid no tax on income from the 1994 Farnham tour. Pollstar News said that when his offices were raided the previous year he had promised to give evidence against others in the scheme in exchange for avoiding jail, and that the DPP had initially agreed but then changed its position.

Other accounts give a different figure. Crikey wrote in July 2007 that the sentence was two and a half years, with half of it suspended. Obituaries Australia, writing in 2022, described a 15-month sentence. The Music Network said he "eventually served 15 months in jail". SBS News, reporting his death, said he spent about 10 months in jail in 2007. These accounts cannot all be reconciled from the reports available, and they are set out here as reported.

Pollstar News said that members of the legal profession believed the sentence was harsh because of Wheatley's public profile. It said Wheatley had told close friends he expected some jail time, but not as much as he received. Crikey reported that representatives of the Australian Crime Commission at the trial appeared shocked at the severity of the sentence.

Within days of the sentence, Wheatley's lawyers filed to appeal its severity, according to Pollstar News. Crikey reported in November 2007 that the appeal was heard in the Victorian Court of Appeal and that Justice Alex Chernov, one of the three judges on the bench, told the court it had the power to increase the sentence if the original one were set aside, and warned that it could feel compelled to do so. Crikey said legal sources believed Justice Chernov should have stood aside, because he had already heard the application for leave to appeal as a single judge.

Crikey's account was that Wheatley wanted to press on, confident of a lesser sentence, while his wife, Gaynor, was not prepared to risk more time apart from him. Richter went back before the bench and said the only course left was to ask for leave to drop the appeal. Crikey reported that Wheatley would stay in jail for another 11 months, and that he was unhappy working in the factory at the minimum-security Beechworth prison.

Wheatley's management career continued after the case. Obituaries Australia says he remained John Farnham's manager until the end of his life. It also says he was the manager who discovered Delta Goodrem when she was in her early teens and helped get her 2003 debut, Innocent Eyes, released; Obituaries Australia counts it among the best-selling albums the ARIA charts have recorded. Obituaries Australia adds that Goodrem chose not to renew her contract with him the same year.

The Music Network reported that character statements from several public figures were given at the trial, including the entertainer Bert Newton and the future Governor-General Peter Cosgrove. Its article does not say what weight the court gave them.

Wheatley died in Melbourne on Tuesday, 1 February 2022, aged 74, from complications of COVID-19. SBS News reported that he had been hospitalised with the virus. He is survived by his wife, Gaynor, and their children Tim, Samantha and Kara. The Masters Apprentices said on Facebook that he "left his mark forever on Australian Music". Glenn Shorrock, who sang with Wheatley-managed Little River Band, told ABC Breakfast that Wheatley had fought for better royalty rates for struggling musicians. Entertainment reporter Richard Wilkins called him one of the founding fathers of the Australian music industry, and named him as one of three key industry pioneers to die in the past year, alongside the INXS manager Chris Murphy and the Mushroom record founder Michael Gudinski.

Wheatley's obituaries give two very different measures of him. One is commercial and cultural: a manager who turned Farnham's career around, took a financial risk that paid off commercially, and fought, in the words of fellow musicians, for better royalty rates. The other is the court record: a man who pleaded guilty to hiding income offshore, who said in open court that he regretted it, and who spent part of his sentence behind bars. The two strands run side by side in the reporting. The accounts agree that he pleaded guilty and was jailed, but they do not agree on the length of the sentence or how long he served, and the dispute over the prosecution's conduct was raised by his own lawyers and by Crikey, and the appeal that could have tested the sentence was dropped.
